body:
I was thinking of taking a stab at this problem. It seems to me at there are three approaches to solving it:
1. Copy the old undo file and give it some extension like `.bak`. If the same problem happens again (there is a .bak already, but we need to copy the current version of the undo file), delete the old .bak and move the current undo file to have the .bak extension.
2. Copy the old undo file and give it some extension like `.bak0`. If the problem occurs again, create a `.bak1` and keep incrementing the number as many times as is necessary.
3. Merge the old undo history file with the one that is about to be written. This is more complex, but prevents creating extra files.

Regardless of how this problem is solved, I don't think that it's covered in the tests right now, so I should also create tests for this case, yes?

Which of the above (or any alternative) approaches seems like the right one for this problem?

@justinmk `vim_tempname` does not look like a good idea for the job like this: /tmp _is cleared upon system initialization_, so is absolutely useless for recovering anything on system crash. I actually do not know why most suggestions from previous message start with “copy the old undo file”: “do mv” from the first message looks better. Probably it makes sense to reuse ShaDa code for this, it already does “write new ShaDa file to {fname}.tmp.a, then rename upon success”.

I'm sorry for the abiguity

> Copy the old undo file

was intended to be the equivalent of `mv`ing it, not having two. That was poorly worded.
@ZyX-I Which part of the ShaDa code should I look at? It sounds like the functionality that I want already does exist.

@whereswaldon The idea of safe overwriting is
1. Write new file to a temporary location.
2. Upon successfull write move it onto a permanent location.

(2) is atomic as long as files are on the same filesystem, and even otherwise is rather safe: depending on where process was interrupted you may get
- Partial or absent new version in temporary location.
- New (temporary location) and old (permament location) versions at once.
- New version at permanent location which is what was intended.
- Part of the new version in permanent location and full new version in temporary location (assuming that temporary file is in another file system).

This is used by ShaDa code, I also had some an impression that some combination of &backup* options will yield the same behaviour, but after rereading documentation am not sure that there exists such combination. Behaviour is coded in `shada_write_file()`, see `shada_write_file_open` label.

Though ShaDa code has more then one reason to behave like it does: it not only needs to write a new version, it also needs to read the old one. Temporary file is not used if you have chosen to ignore the old file!

Though you may choose to ignore the old file only by explicitly using `wshada!` (with bang), so system crash leaving truncated file is rather unlikely. But this may happen in case of crash during `wshada!`.
Vim has the same problem with `wviminfo!` (with bang) AFAIR.
@justinmk What do you think about moving the relevant code to `file_open` and `file_close`, protected by `FILE_USE_TEMP`? (I am referring to #4865.)

@ZyX-I So the idea with this particular issue would be to write the new version of the undo file to a temporary location, and then `mv` the old version of the undo file to some safe backup location before finally moving the new version of the undo file to where it ought to be?

With regards to

>  Instead of using a naming scheme like .bak, use the existing vim_tempname function to create a temporary file.

and

> `vim_tempname` does not look like a good idea for the job like this: `/tmp` is cleared upon system initialization, so is absolutely useless for recovering anything on system crash.

In this case, the problem is that the old file is deleted _after_ the system reboot and you reopen vim and re`:write` the file(unless I'm fundamentally misunderstanding the issue). In that case, moving the file to `/tmp` does seem fine, since the user will presumably realize the problem and recover their file before the system is restarted again.

Do you think it's worth warning the user when this kind of backup of the undo history occurs? I have no idea how common such a scenario is outside of the extreme case that brought this issue to light in the first place. I assume that the original code deleted the old version of the undo file for a reason?
